sentences.text: The first thing that came up that summer came up on Jonas's fourth day.
It was a shoe.
A small leather shoe, the kind a child of maybe two years old would wear, with tiny worn buttons on the side.
Jonas found it himself, in the field behind the barn, when he was walking and looking down at the wet grass and half-thinking about nothing.
He did not touch it.
He ran back to the house.
Aunt Sigrún came with him, walking without hurrying, and when she saw the shoe she nodded, like she had been expecting something exactly like this.
She had a small trowel with her.
She dug around the shoe very carefully.
She lifted it out.
She turned it over in her hands.
She put it in a cloth bag.
The next day they drove to the village.
Aunt Sigrún went into three houses, and Jonas waited in the car for the first two, but the third time she came out and said, "Come in with me.

I want you to see how this works." And so Jonas went in, and he sat on a small footstool in the corner of a very warm kitchen while an old woman with a scarf around her head held the shoe in her hands and turned it over.
The old woman did not speak for a very long time.
And then she said, in Icelandic, and Aunt Sigrún translated for Jonas: "This is Ástrós's.
My sister.
She was two years old.
She lost it in the summer of 1942.
She would not stop crying.
My mother went out with a lantern that night, and she looked, and she could not find it.
And my sister cried all the next day too.
And in the end my mother knitted her a new pair of woolen booties, and Ástrós forgot about the shoe." The old woman looked up.
Her eyes were wet, but she was smiling.
"Ástrós died last winter.
She was eighty-three.
I will bring her the shoe." And she reached out and took it, and pressed it against her chest, and Jonas understood, then, that this was the point.
This was what the whole shelf was for.
The doll came up two weeks later, near the stone wall behind the house.
This one Aunt Sigrún found.
It was small and porcelain and its dress had rotted away and one arm was missing.
In the village, no one knew who it belonged to.
"That happens too," Aunt Sigrún said.
"Sometimes the memory is gone.
Sometimes the family moved away.
Sometimes it is very old — older than anyone alive.
Then I just write down where I found it and when, and I keep it.
Maybe someone will come one day.
Maybe not."
She wrote a new tag for the doll.
Summer 2026.
From the stone wall behind the house.
Owner unknown.
She tied the tag on with string and put the doll on the shelf, in an empty space between the fountain pen and the small tin box.
Jonas watched her do this and thought about how much time she must have spent, over the years, doing exactly this.
Writing tags.
Tying string.
Making room.
The third thing came up in the second week of July.
It was a fountain pen.
Silver, tarnished, with the initials E.
S.
G.
engraved on the cap.
Aunt Sigrún held it for a moment when Jonas brought it to her, and her face changed a little.
"This one I know," she said.
S.
G.
is my mother.
Elsa Sveinsdóttir Grímsdóttir.
She lost this pen writing a letter in the yard in 1957.
She looked for it for a week.
She always said it was her favorite thing."
She wrote the tag for it very slowly.
When she was done she held the pen for a long moment before she put it on the shelf.
Jonas thought she might cry, but she did not.
She only stood there quietly, and then she went back into the kitchen, and he heard her fill the kettle for tea, the way she did every afternoon at four o'clock.
That evening at supper Jonas asked her something he had been thinking about.
"Do you ever want to keep them?
Not give them back.
When you know who they belong to." Aunt Sigrún thought about this for a long time before she answered.
"I want to," she said.
"Every time.
It is very hard to give them back.
But they were never mine.
They were only kept by me for a while.
That is the difference."
Jonas looked at his soup.
Then he looked at her.
"Have you ever kept one anyway?" he asked.
Aunt Sigrún smiled a small tired smile.
"Once," she said.
"I kept one once, for a year.
And then I gave it back.
It was the pen.
My mother had died the winter before.
And I wanted to hold on to it.
But eventually I gave it to her sister, who is the last person alive who remembers her.
And a year after that, her sister died.
And then it came back to me." She lifted her tea.
"Everything comes back around eventually.
If you are patient."
